summary: This informational memo defines MIB objects for managing RADIUS accounting servers. It replaces RFC 2621 by deprecating the IPv4-only table and adding one supporting version-neutral IP addresses, and adds UNITS and REFERENCE clauses to some objects.

plainLanguage.summary: The accounting server is the clerk who files records of network use. This is a dashboard for watching the clerk, updated to handle newer style addresses.

questions: what is the radius accounting server mib
subtitle: A management database for watching how a RADIUS accounting server handles requests from its clients, now able to hold IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The earlier RADIUS accounting server MIB, RFC 2621, could only record client addresses in an IPv4-only format.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4671 deprecates the IPv4-only table and adds radiusAccClientExtTable with version-neutral address types, carries the other objects forward and adds UNITS and REFERENCE clauses.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2621. It is an Informational memo, and its client-side partner is RFC 4670.

today: RFC 4671 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2621, and it has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. The matching client-side MIB is RFC 4670.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4671 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing RADIUS accounting servers. The MIB module is written in SMIv2, and its objects are generally accessed through SNMP. It relates to the accounting protocol of RFC 2866, in which clients send Accounting-Requests and servers reply with Accounting-Responses.

RADIUS accounting servers would be expected to implement this server MIB, while NAS devices would implement the client MIB defined in RFC 4670.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a set of gauges a network manager can read to see how an accounting server is doing.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 2621
sections.content:
This memo obsoletes RFC 2621. It deprecates the radiusAccClientTable table and adds a new table, radiusAccClientExtTable, containing radiusAccClientInetAddressType and radiusAccClientInetAddress. These objects support version-neutral IP addressing formats, replacing the old radiusAccClientAddress.

The RFC follows the advice quoted from RFC 4001: define new tables with the version-neutral textual conventions, mark the new tables current and the old ones deprecated, and avoid keeping multiple similar tables for different IP versions. The remaining objects are carried forward, with UNITS and REFERENCE clauses added to selected ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The old guest list could only hold short addresses. A new list holds any kind, and the old one gets a 'do not use' sticker.

sections.title: Structure of the Module
sections.content:
The module has thirteen scalars and one table, listing the accounting clients with which the server shares a secret, one row per client. The scalars include an identification string for the server software, its up time and reset time in hundredths of a second, a configuration reset control, and server-wide totals such as total requests, duplicate requests, responses, malformed requests, bad authenticators, packets dropped, requests with no records and unknown types.

An entity that is both client and server, such as a RADIUS proxy, is expected to support this server MIB and the client MIB of RFC 4670.
sections.plainLanguage: The server keeps one big scoreboard for everything it handles, plus a small card for each sender.

sections.title: Per-Client Counters and the Reset Control
sections.content:
Each client row has a client address, an identifier, and counters for that client: packets dropped, requests, duplicate requests, responses, bad authenticators, malformed requests, requests with no records and unknown types. The new table adds radiusAccServerCounterDiscontinuity, a time value since the last discontinuity in the counters.

The one writable object is radiusAccServConfigReset. Setting it to reset(2) reinitializes any persistent server state as if the server had just been started. When read, it returns other(1), initializing(3) or running(4), and never reset(2).
sections.plainLanguage: Each sender gets its own score card. There is also one big reset button, which only trusted people should press.

sections.title: Keeping the Deprecated Table
sections.content:
A managed entity MAY keep supporting the deprecated table if it only supports IPv4 addresses, or if it supports both versions and keeps the table for older management stations. In the second case this SHOULD only be done when the addresses in the new table are IPv4 and can be represented accurately in both tables.

Entities SHOULD NOT create rows in the deprecated table for a client whose address is not IPv4, and SHOULD NOT return inaccurate addresses or SNMP access errors for IPv4-only objects. If a client appears in both tables, the row indexes SHOULD match.
sections.plainLanguage: The old list can stay for old viewers, but it must never show a wrong address, and matching entries should share a row number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unlike the client MIB, this one has a read-write object, radiusAccServConfigReset. Abuse of it may lead to a Denial of Service attack on the server, because resetting may or may not interrupt processing of pending requests, depending on the implementation. The client address objects are also sensitive, since they could help someone mount an attack on the accounting client.

Every object in this MIB is read-only except where noted, and the RFC points to SNMPv3 for protection. It recommends that implementers consider the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The RFC says it is important to control even GET access to the sensitive objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The reset button could be used to knock the server over, and the client list shows who talks to it, so only the right people should have access.
